Bayesian stability models: Eberhart-Russell, Finlay-Wilkinson and Shukla

Muhammad Yaseen

2026-11-05

Source: vignettes/bayesammi_10_stability_models.qmd

\[ \newcommand{\vy}{\mathbf{y}} \newcommand{\vx}{\mathbf{x}} \newcommand{\vb}{\mathbf{b}} \newcommand{\ve}{\mathbf{e}} \newcommand{\vone}{\mathbf{1}} \newcommand{\vbeta}{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \newcommand{\vmu}{\boldsymbol{\mu}} \newcommand{\mX}{\mathbf{X}} \newcommand{\mZ}{\mathbf{Z}} \newcommand{\mV}{\mathbf{V}} \newcommand{\mI}{\mathbf{I}} \newcommand{\mJ}{\mathbf{J}} \newcommand{\mSigma}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} \newcommand{\mY}{\mathbf{Y}} \newcommand{\mK}{\mathbf{K}} \newcommand{\mH}{\mathbf{H}} \newcommand{\va}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} \newcommand{\vg}{\boldsymbol{\gamma}} \newcommand{\vt}{\boldsymbol{\tau}} \newcommand{\vd}{\boldsymbol{\delta}} \newcommand{\vtheta}{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \newcommand{\vv}{\mathbf{v}} \newcommand{\E}{\mathrm{E}} \newcommand{\Var}{\mathrm{Var}} \newcommand{\Cov}{\mathrm{Cov}} \newcommand{\tr}{\operatorname{tr}} \]

1 Abstract

The joint regression of Finlay and Wilkinson (1963) and Eberhart and Russell (1966) and the stability variance of Shukla (1972) are the most used measures of adaptability and stability. Their classical estimates come with tests, not with the uncertainty a breeder needs to choose. bayes_stability() fits the three models by Gibbs sampling, so every slope, deviation variance and stability variance has a posterior distribution. This vignette gives the model, the sampler, an analysis of Maiz, a comparison of the three models and the safety-first index of Eskridge (1990).

2 Model

For genotype \(i\), environment \(j\) and plot \(l\), \[y_{ijl} = \mu + g_i + (1 + b_i)h_j + d_{ij} + e_{ijl}, \qquad d_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{d,i}), \quad e_{ijl} \sim N(0, \sigma^2),\] with \(\sum_i g_i = \sum_j h_j = \sum_i b_i = 0\). The environmental index \(h_j\) is a parameter, estimated jointly with the others, as in the Bayesian Finlay-Wilkinson regression of Lian and de los Campos (2016). The classical analysis plugs in the environment means instead and so ignores their error. The slope of genotype \(i\) is \(1 + b_i\), with average 1.

.model Slopes Deviation variance Classical counterpart
"ER" yes \(\sigma^2_{d,i}\) for every genotype Eberhart and Russell (1966); Bayesian version of Oliveira et al. (2018)
"FW" yes one \(\sigma^2_d\) Finlay and Wilkinson (1963)
"Shukla" no (\(b_i = 0\)) \(\sigma^2_{d,i}\) for every genotype: the stability variance Shukla (1972); Edwards and Jannink (2006)

The replicates separate the deviations \(d_{ij}\) from the plot error \(e_{ijl}\), so the data must have replicates.

2.1 Priors

bam_stab_priors() sets normal priors on \(\mu\) and on the contrasts \(\mK_G\mathbf{g}\), \(\mK_E\mathbf{h}\) and \(\mK_G\mathbf{b}\) (so the sums are zero), and scaled inverse chi-squared priors on \(\sigma^2\) and \(\sigma^2_{d,i}\). The defaults are vague and in the unit of the trait: \(10^4\) times the variance of the response for the effects, and the least-squares variances as scales with one degree of freedom.

bam_stab_priors(
    mu_var = NULL
  , g_var  = NULL
  , h_var  = NULL
  , b_var  = 100
  , nu     = 1
  , s2     = NULL
  , nu_d   = 1
  , s2_d   = NULL
  )
Priors of the Bayesian stability models
  mu       ~ N(0, 1e4 x var(y))
  K_G g    ~ N(0, 1e4 x var(y) I)
  K_E h    ~ N(0, 1e4 x var(y) I)
  K_G b    ~ N(0, 100 I)   (slopes 1 + b_i)
  sigma^2  ~ Inv-chi^2(1, within-cell mean square)
  sigma_d^2 ~ Inv-chi^2(1, least-squares deviation variance)

2.2 The sampler

Every conditional distribution is normal or scaled inverse chi-squared. Drawing the deviations \(d_{ij}\) one at a time next to the genotype effects would mix slowly, because the mean of the deviations of a genotype and its effect \(g_i\) trade off. The sampler therefore draws \(\mu\), \(\mathbf{g}\), \(\mathbf{h}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) with the deviations integrated out: each observed cell mean then has variance \(\sigma^2_{d,i} + \sigma^2/n_{ij}\). The deviations come next, then the variances. This is a partially collapsed Gibbs sampler: each sweep is still an exact draw from the posterior. Unbalanced data need nothing more, as the weights use the number of plots of every cell, and an empty cell has weight zero. The sampler is compiled; vignette 13 checks it against a plain R version.

3 The Eberhart-Russell model on Maiz 

fs <-
  bayes_stability(
      .data   = Maiz
    , .y      = y
    , .gen    = entry
    , .env    = site
    , .rep    = rep
    , .model  = "ER"
    , .nIter  = 3000
    , .burnin = 500
    , .thin   = 1
    , .chains = 2
    , .priors = bam_stab_priors(
          mu_var = NULL
        , g_var  = NULL
        , h_var  = NULL
        , b_var  = 100
        , nu     = 1
        , s2     = NULL
        , nu_d   = 1
        , s2_d   = NULL
        )
    , .level  = 0.95
    , .alpha  = 0.05
    , .seed   = 1
    , .waic   = TRUE
    )

The slopes of genotypes 4 and 5 lie above 1 with 95% posterior probability: they respond more than the average genotype to good environments. The slope of 8 lies below 1. The posterior probability that a slope exceeds 1 is in the column prob_slope_above_1. A breeder can use it directly, which a test of \(b_i = 1\) does not allow.

plot(x = fs, which = "slopes")
plot(x = fs, which = "lines")
plot(x = fs, which = "deviations")

The deviation variances are poorly determined from 20 environments, so their HPD intervals are wide and overlap. The Bayesian analysis shows this directly; a classical F test of \(\sigma^2_{d,i} = 0\) would hide it.

3.1 Least squares and Bayes 

data.table::data.table(
    Gen        = s$Gen
  , slope_ls   = round(x = fs$ls$slope, digits = 3)
  , slope      = round(x = s$slope, digits = 3)
  , dev_var_ls = round(fs$ls$dev_var)
  , dev_var    = round(s$dev_var)
  )

The posterior means of the slopes are close to the least-squares slopes (correlation 0.997). The deviation variances differ more. The posterior of a variance estimated from 20 environments is skewed to the right, so its mean lies above its mode. The prior, with its scale at the pooled least-squares value, also pulls the small variances up. The order of the genotypes changes less (rank correlation 0.73).

4 The safety-first index

Eskridge (1990) ranks genotypes by a lower quantile of their yield across environments, \(\mu + g_i - z_{1-\alpha}\sqrt{V_i}\), where \(V_i\) is the variance of genotype \(i\) across environments under the model:

Model \(V_i\)
Eberhart-Russell \(b_i^2 s^2_h (1 - 1/E) + \sigma^2_{d,i}\)
Finlay-Wilkinson \(b_i^2 s^2_h (1 - 1/E)\)
Shukla \(s^2_h + \sigma^2_{d,i}\)

Here \(s^2_h\) is the variance of the environmental index. The index is computed on every draw, so it has an HPD interval and every genotype has a probability of being the best on it. Here 6 is most probably the best (0.84).

ff <-
  bayes_stability(
      .data   = Maiz
    , .y      = y
    , .gen    = entry
    , .env    = site
    , .rep    = rep
    , .model  = "FW"
    , .nIter  = 3000
    , .burnin = 500

    , .level  = 0.95
    , .alpha  = 0.05
    , .seed   = 1
    , .waic   = TRUE
    )
cp <-
  bam_compare(
      ER     = fs
    , FW     = ff
    , Shukla = fh

WAIC prefers the ER model; the next, FW, is 4 above it (0.8 standard errors of the difference). The standard errors do not separate the three models here; the choice can follow the question, the slopes for adaptability and the variances for stability. The models are fitted to the same plots, so they can also be compared with the AMMI and GGE fits of bayes_ammi() (vignette 9).

7 Interpretation and sources 

bam_interpret(
    x             = fs
  , higher_better = TRUE
  , top           = 5
  )
Bayesian Eberhart-Russell stability model

Best by the safety-first index (alpha = 0.05): 6, 5, 9, 3 and 4; most
probably the best: 6 (0.84).

Findings:
- The chains have converged (largest potential scale reduction factor 1.017;
  smallest effective sample size of the main parameters 574).
- Slopes whose HPD interval lies above 1 (respond more than average to good
  environments): 4 and 5; below 1 (respond less, relatively better in poor
  environments): 8.
- Smallest deviation variance: 6 (77,600); largest: 1 (483,000).
- Share of each genotype's variation explained by the regression (R2): 1
  0.73, 2 0.87, 3 0.92, 4 0.94, 5 0.95, 6 0.96, 7 0.88, 8 0.57, 9 0.94.

Recommendations:
- For a wide recommendation choose genotypes with a high mean, a slope near 1
  and a small deviation variance; for favourable environments a slope above 1
  with a high mean.
- The safety-first index combines the two: 6, 5 and 9 lead.

Cautions:
- The environmental index is estimated from the same trial; with few
  environments the slopes are uncertain (see the HPD intervals).
